title: Judge quashes trial of Toronto cop accused of ignoring teen's suicide
article: A Toronto cop who refused to help save a young man from committing suicide won't stand trial on a breach of trust charge as a judge ruled the policeman's actions don't constitute a breach of trust.
Justice Maureen Forestell quashed the committal for trial against Const. Kyle Upjohn, saying "there was no evidence capable of" concluding he intended to commit a breach of trust.
Last April a lower court committed Upjohn, 34, to stand trial but Forestell's decision quashes that ruling.
Crown attorney Peter Scrutton argued Upjohn did the opposite of what police officers should do: Save people's lives.

"When Upjohn was apprised of information that someone's life was in danger, that someone needed saving and, though duty-bound to assist, did the opposite - he ignored the entreaty and literally drove the other way, apparently aimlessly for 12 minutes," Scrutton stated in his factum.
"If any breach of a duty is a departure from the standard expected of a police officer...this shocking, intentional decision to withhold services is," he concluded.
On Feb. 6, 2016, a concerned citizen told Upjohn, as he sat in his cruiser, that a young man was preparing to hang himself in High Park.
Shortly after, Alexandre Boucher, 19, was found dead.
Upjohn, a member of the service for 10 years, has been suspended since May 2016.

Ontario's Special Investigations Unit charged Upjohn with criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessities of life, but the charges were later dropped by the Crown because it felt it couldn't establish the exact time of death.
Upjohn was then charged with breach of trust - a charge laid when an official is accused of breaching his responsibilities as a public official.

In his factum, Scrutton argued Upjohn lied to the citizen that he was on a call and told the citizen to phone 911. Upjohn drove away "until he was specifically dispatched to the attempt suicide occurrence created when that citizen phoned 911.

"This was not an innocent mistake. Upjohn masked his failure to act with dishonesty - by lying about being 'on a call.' The lie suggests that Upjohn knew what he was doing wrong, that he was intentionally using his office for a purpose other than the public good," Scrutton said.

Upjohn appealed the committal to stand trial decision, asserting that the breach of trust charge did not apply because there had to be evidence that he had a corrupt or dishonest ulterior purpose for avoiding the call.
The officer's lawyer, Gary Clewley, said his client was negligent "for driving away," but it was "an avoidance of his duty, not a commission.
It demonstrated "indifference or even laziness, not corruption or dishonesty," he added.
Uphohn is being prosecuted for three counts of professional misconduct under Ontario's Police Services Act, including neglect of duty.
But Clewley argued there was no evidence Upjohn intended to use his position as an officer for a dishonest, corrupt or oppressive purpose, which is a necessary element of the breach offence.
Forestell was persuaded by Clewley's argument, saying while Upjohn may have "put his own comfort or needs before the good of the public," this was "not enough" evidence to prove a breach of trust.
It's unknown whether the decision will be appealed.
